items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "lithosphere".
items.answer: The rigid outer layer of the Earth, made of the crust and uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the rigid outer layer of the Earth, made of the crust and uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between a divergent boundary and a convergent boundary.
items.answer: At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms (Mid-Atlantic Ridge); at convergent boundaries plates move together and crust is destroyed by subduction or crumpled by collision (Andes, Himalayas).
items.markingKey: At divergent boundaries plates move apart and new crust forms (Mid-Atlantic Ridge); at convergent boundaries plates move together and crust is destroyed by subduction or crumpled by collision (Andes, Himalayas). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "All earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Hotspots (Hawaii, Yellowstone) and intraplate faults (e.g. the 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes) occur away from boundaries.
items.markingKey: Hotspots (Hawaii, Yellowstone) and intraplate faults (e.g. the 1811-12 New Madrid earthquakes) occur away from boundaries. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Between 2004 and 2024 the population of a suburb of Lima changed from 1,219,720 to 1,738,350 people. Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (1,738,350 − 1,219,720) ÷ 1,219,720 × 100; A1 +42.5% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.stem:
Refer to the data below.

Map description: a world map shows narrow belts of earthquake epicentres along the margins of the Pacific Ocean, the mid-ocean ridges and from the Mediterranean through Iran to the Himalayas, with isolated volcanoes in Hawaii and Yellowstone.

Explain the isolated volcanoes shown on the map.
items.answer: Hawaii and Yellowstone are above mantle plumes (hotspots), where heat rising from deep in the mantle melts the overlying plate.
items.markingKey: Hawaii and Yellowstone are above mantle plumes (hotspots), where heat rising from deep in the mantle melts the overlying plate. Award 1 mark per valid point or correct step, up to [3]; data quoted must include units; points must be drawn from the resource.

items.stem: Suggest why Iceland has both volcanoes and frequent small earthquakes.
items.answer: It lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where plates diverge and also above a hotspot, so magma rises easily and rifting causes shallow earthquakes.
items.markingKey: It lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge where plates diverge and also above a hotspot, so magma rises easily and rifting causes shallow earthquakes.

items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "Plate tectonic theory fully explains the global distribution of geophysical hazards."
items.answer: Plate tectonics explains most volcanic and seismic hazards, but not all geophysical hazards.
items.markingKey: For: most earthquakes and volcanoes lie along boundaries (Ring of Fire). Against: hotspots and intraplate earthquakes need additional explanation (mantle plumes). [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: Explain the internal structure of the Earth and how it causes movement of tectonic plates.
items.answer: Indicative content: Crust, mantle (lithosphere, asthenosphere), outer and inner core; heat from radioactive decay; convection, slab pull, ridge push; boundary types with examples.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Crust, mantle (lithosphere, asthenosphere), outer and inner core; heat from radioactive decay; convection, slab pull, ridge push; boundary types with examples. items.stem: Explain how a hotspot produces a chain of volcanoes.
items.answer: A stationary mantle plume melts the lithosphere above it; as the plate moves over the plume, older volcanoes are carried away and become extinct while new ones form above the hotspot, creating a chain (Hawaiian-Emperor chain).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A stationary mantle plume melts the lithosphere above it; as the plate moves over the plume, older volcanoes are carried away and become extinct while new ones form above the hotspot, creating a chain (Hawaiian-Emperor chain). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the lithosphere and the asthenosphere.
items.answer: The lithosphere is the rigid crust and upper mantle forming plates; the asthenosphere is the hotter, weaker, partially molten mantle layer below on which the plates move.
items.markingKey: The lithosphere is the rigid crust and upper mantle forming plates; the asthenosphere is the hotter, weaker, partially molten mantle layer below on which the plates move. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to the Peru-Chile Trench, explain how it illustrates oceanic-continental subduction.
items.answer: The Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America, producing the Andes and earthquakes such as Maule 2010 (Mw 8.8) Subduction generates both magma for volcanoes and stress for great earthquakes.
items.markingKey: Context (The Nazca Plate subducts beneath South America, producing the Andes and earthquakes such as Maule 2010 (Mw 8.8)) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Subduction generates both magma for volcanoes and stress for great earthquakes. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to oceanic-continental subduction.

items.stem: A seismic network in New Zealand records on average 400 earthquakes of magnitude ≥ 4.5 per year. Assuming the Gutenberg-Richter relationship with b = 1 (ten times fewer earthquakes for each unit increase in magnitude), estimate the number of earthquakes of magnitude ≥ 6.5 per year and the average recurrence interval of such an event.
items.answer: 400 / 10^2 = 4 per year; recurrence interval ≈ 0.25 years
items.markingKey: M1 divide by 10^(ΔM); A1 4 per year; A1 recurrence 0.25 years.

items.stem: Each step on the VEI scale represents about how much more erupted material?
items.answer: Ten times
items.markingKey: Ten times. The scale is logarithmic above VEI 2.

items.stem: "A higher VEI always means more deaths." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Deaths depend on population exposure and preparedness; Pinatubo (VEI 6) killed about 850 thanks to evacuation, whereas Nevado del Ruiz (VEI 3) killed about 23,000.
items.markingKey: Deaths depend on population exposure and preparedness; Pinatubo (VEI 6) killed about 850 thanks to evacuation, whereas Nevado del Ruiz (VEI 3) killed about 23,000. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why gas content is important in determining the type of eruption.
items.answer: Dissolved gases (water vapour, CO₂) expand as magma rises; if they cannot escape, they fragment magma into ash and drive explosive Plinian eruptions; low gas or easy escape gives effusive eruptions.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Dissolved gases (water vapour, CO₂) expand as magma rises; if they cannot escape, they fragment magma into ash and drive explosive Plinian eruptions; low gas or easy escape gives effusive eruptions. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

A: 47.6, 352; B: 29.2, 734; C: 19.0, 636; D: 39.5, 599; E: 51.0, 211; F: 14.9, 884.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 6: 0.829).

items.stem: The 1815 eruption of Tambora, Indonesia (VEI 7) led to:
options: the end of the last glacial period
the Little Ice Age beginning in 1300
"the year without a summer" in 1816
the 2004 tsunami
items.answer: "the year without a summer" in 1816
items.markingKey: C. Crop failures and famine occurred in Europe and North America.

items.stem: Distinguish between effusive eruptions and explosive eruptions.
items.answer: Effusive eruptions release fluid lava flows with low gas pressure (Kīlauea); explosive eruptions fragment viscous, gas-rich magma into ash, pumice and pyroclastic flows (Pinatubo).
items.markingKey: Effusive eruptions release fluid lava flows with low gas pressure (Kīlauea); explosive eruptions fragment viscous, gas-rich magma into ash, pumice and pyroclastic flows (Pinatubo). items.stem: An eruption of a stratovolcano in the Andes ejected about 93.3 km³ of tephra. The VEI scale is logarithmic: VEI 2 ≥ 0.001 km³, VEI 3 ≥ 0.01, VEI 4 ≥ 0.1, VEI 5 ≥ 1, VEI 6 ≥ 10, VEI 7 ≥ 100 km³. Assign the eruption a VEI. How does its ejected volume compare with Tambora 1815 (about 150.0 km³)?
items.answer: VEI 6; 93.3 / 150.0 = 0.622 times the volume of Tambora 1815
items.markingKey: A1 VEI 6 (93.3 km³ lies between 10 and 100 km³). A1 ratio 0.622.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "focus (hypocentre)"?
options: The point within the Earth where an earthquake rupture begins
The internal resistance of slope materials to movement, from friction and cohesion
The rapid downslope movement of a mass of rock or soil along a shear plane
The rigid outer layer of the Earth, made of the crust and uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates
items.answer: The point within the Earth where an earthquake rupture begins
items.markingKey: A. "focus (hypocentre)" is the point within the Earth where an earthquake rupture begins.

items.stem: "A magnitude 8 earthquake releases twice as much energy as a magnitude 4 earthquake." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The scale is logarithmic: four units difference is about 31.6⁴ ≈ 1,000,000 times more energy.
items.markingKey: The scale is logarithmic: four units difference is about 31.6⁴ ≈ 1,000,000 times more energy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how earthquakes are caused by elastic rebound.
items.answer: Plates are locked by friction while moving; strain energy builds in rocks either side of the fault; when stress exceeds friction the fault slips suddenly and the rocks rebound, releasing energy as seismic waves.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Plates are locked by friction while moving; strain energy builds in rocks either side of the fault; when stress exceeds friction the fault slips suddenly and the rocks rebound, releasing energy as seismic waves. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Suggest why the 2011 Christchurch earthquake (Mw 6.2) was more damaging than the larger 2010 Darfield earthquake (Mw 7.1).
items.answer: Its focus was shallow (about 5 km) and close to the city centre; strong vertical acceleration; liquefaction of soft sediments; buildings were already weakened in 2010; it struck at lunchtime.
items.markingKey: Its focus was shallow (about 5 km) and close to the city centre; strong vertical acceleration; liquefaction of soft sediments; buildings were already weakened in 2010; it struck at lunchtime.

items.stem: Distinguish between magnitude and intensity.
items.answer: Magnitude measures the energy released at the source and has one value per earthquake; intensity describes the effects of shaking at a particular location and varies from place to place.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "factor of safety"?
options: The ratio of shear strength to shear stress on a slope; values below 1 indicate likely failure
The rapid downslope movement of a mass of rock or soil along a shear plane
The sudden release of strain energy stored in rocks as a fault ruptures, causing an earthquake
The downslope movement of rock, regolith or snow under the influence of gravity
items.answer: The ratio of shear strength to shear stress on a slope; values below 1 indicate likely failure
items.markingKey: A. "factor of safety" is the ratio of shear strength to shear stress on a slope; values below 1 indicate likely failure.

items.stem: A student claims: "Planting vegetation always stops landslides." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Roots increase cohesion near the surface, but deep-seated failures and intense rainfall can still cause landslides on vegetated slopes.
items.markingKey: Roots increase cohesion near the surface, but deep-seated failures and intense rainfall can still cause landslides on vegetated slopes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: At a road cutting in Kerala, the shear strength of the regolith is 70 kPa and the shear stress acting down the slope is 36 kPa. Calculate the factor of safety (strength ÷ stress). Intense rainfall then raises pore-water pressure, reducing shear strength by 20%. Calculate the new factor of safety and state whether the slope is likely to fail.
items.answer: FS = 70/36 = 1.94; after rain FS = 56.0/36 = 1.56; stable (FS ≥ 1)
items.markingKey: A1 FS 1.94; M1 strength reduced by 20%; A1 FS 1.56; R1 FS < 1 means failure.

items.stem: Give one strength and one weakness of the claim that engineering is the most effective way to manage landslide risk.
items.answer: Engineering works best for high-value urban slopes; planning and warnings are essential elsewhere.
items.markingKey: For: Hong Kong's slope programme cut deaths dramatically. Against: expensive; not affordable for poor communities. items.stem: Explain why earthquakes often trigger landslides in mountainous regions.
items.answer: Ground shaking temporarily increases shear stress and can cause liquefaction or loosening of regolith on steep slopes, e.g. tens of thousands of landslides after the 2008 Sichuan and 2015 Gorkha earthquakes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Ground shaking temporarily increases shear stress and can cause liquefaction or loosening of regolith on steep slopes, e.g. tens of thousands of landslides after the 2008 Sichuan and 2015 Gorkha earthquakes. items.stem: With reference to the 1970 Huascarán avalanche, Peru, explain how it illustrates earthquake-triggered mass movement.
items.answer: An earthquake loosened ice and rock that fell from Huascarán and buried Yungay, killing about 20,000 people. Shaking released a huge mass of ice and rock that travelled at very high speed.
items.markingKey: Context (An earthquake loosened ice and rock that fell from Huascarán and buried Yungay, killing about 20,000 people.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. The downslope movement of rock, regolith or snow under the influence of gravity
A convergent boundary where a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath another plate, forming an ocean trench
The rigid outer layer of the Earth, made of the crust and uppermost mantle, broken into tectonic plates

items.stem: Which seismic waves cause most damage at the surface?
items.answer: Surface waves (Love and Rayleigh waves)

items.stem: Explain the difference between shear strength and shear stress.
items.answer: Shear strength is the resistance of slope material to movement; shear stress is the force acting to move material downslope - failure occurs when stress exceeds strength.

items.stem: Suggest two methods to reduce landslide risk on slopes above a city.

items.stem: Explain how human activity can increase the risk of mass movement.
items.answer: Undercutting slopes for roads and buildings, deforestation removing root cohesion, adding weight (buildings, waste tips), leaking water pipes and quarrying all reduce slope stability, e.g. hillside favelas in Rio de Janeiro.

items.stem: Explain why collision boundaries produce earthquakes but few volcanoes.
items.answer: Both plates are continental and too buoyant to subduct deeply, so crust crumples and thickens (Himalayas) causing faulting and earthquakes, but little magma is generated.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Both plates are continental and too buoyant to subduct deeply, so crust crumples and thickens (Himalayas) causing faulting and earthquakes, but little magma is generated. items.stem: Explain how a shield volcano differs in form from a stratovolcano.
items.answer: Fluid basaltic lava flows long distances to build broad, gentle slopes (Mauna Loa); viscous lava and ash layers build steep, symmetrical cones (Fuji, Mayon).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Fluid basaltic lava flows long distances to build broad, gentle slopes (Mauna Loa); viscous lava and ash layers build steep, symmetrical cones (Fuji, Mayon). items.stem: Explain the difference between intensity and magnitude.
items.answer: Magnitude measures the energy released at the source and has one value per earthquake; intensity describes the effects of shaking at a particular location and varies from place to place.

items.stem: Distinguish between rapid mass movements and slow mass movements.
items.answer: Slow movements such as soil creep move millimetres a year and rarely threaten life; rapid ones such as rockfalls, debris flows and avalanches move metres per second and are highly hazardous.

items.stem: Explain how subduction leads to volcanic activity.
items.answer: The descending oceanic plate carries water-rich sediments; at about 100 km depth water is released, lowering the melting point of the overlying mantle wedge, which partially melts; buoyant magma rises to form volcanic arcs such as the Andes or Japan.

items.stem:

A: 12, 6; B: 8, 9; C: 16, 5; D: 23, 13; E: 36, 36; F: 15, 15; G: 33, 30; H: 6, 4.
Calculate Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rs = 1 − 6Σd² / (n³ − n)) and state whether the relationship is significant at the 0.05 level (one-tailed test; critical value for n = 8: 0.643).
